name: Trigger Finger (Stenosing Flexor Tenosynovitis)
summary: A flexor tendon gliding disorder at the A1 pulley causing painful clicking, catching or locking during finger flexion and extension.

looksLike: Finger may lock in flexion, especially in morning
redFlags: Hot swollen digit with fever or suspected infection
Fixed deformity or rapidly progressive dysfunction
firstSteps: Maintain comfortable tendon glide and full finger extension where possible
Consider night splinting in selected early cases

assess: Palpable nodule or tenderness at A1 pulley
Reduced full extension in advanced cases

tests.name: Active Finger Flexion–Extension Observation
tests.purpose: Observe reproducible triggering and identify the involved digit.
tests.positive: Click, catch or lock during tendon excursion with focal A1 pulley symptoms.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Maintain comfortable tendon glide and full finger extension where possible
Consider night splinting in selected early cases
dose: Gentle tendon-glide sequence: 5–10 cycles, 3–5 times/day if not locking painfully
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress graded grip and dexterity without repeated locking
Restore finger ROM and hand function
Coordinate medical options if symptoms persist
dose: Light putty/grip: 2 x 8–12 only when gliding is comfortable
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Return to sustained grip, tool use and sport-specific hand tasks
dose: Functional gripping: short bouts, gradually increasing duration
Progress resistance only if triggering remains controlled
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Grip and dexterity meet daily/work needs

mechanism: Tendon-pulley size mismatch and impaired gliding
Association with diabetes and repetitive gripping
investigations: Usually clinical; imaging is rarely required unless diagnosis is atypical or trauma is suspected.
Medical/hand specialist review for persistent locking or fixed contracture.
manual: Gentle hand mobility may address secondary stiffness.
Do not forcefully manipulate a locked finger or claim massage releases the pulley.
modalities: Splinting may reduce tendon excursion, particularly at night.
Persistent cases may need clinician-led corticosteroid injection or surgical assessment.
mistakes: Forcing a locked finger through painful range
Delaying referral when fixed locking persists
pearls: A1 pulley tenderness plus catching is characteristic.
Exercise is not a substitute for medical management in persistent or fixed locking.

tests.name: Active Finger Flexion–Extension Observation
tests.purpose: Observe reproducible triggering and identify the involved digit.
tests.positive: Click, catch or lock during tendon excursion with focal A1 pulley symptoms.
tests.patientPosition: Patient repeatedly opens and closes hand slowly; clinician palpates A1 pulley at volar MCP region.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Typical clinical pattern; differentiate from joint contracture and tendon injury.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
